subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Putting a business idea into practice

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the role of an entrepreneur?
options: Organising resources, making business decisions and taking risks
Setting national interest rates and controlling inflation
Auditing company accounts on behalf of the government
Guaranteeing that a business will always make a profit
questions.explain: An entrepreneur organises the factors of production, makes key business decisions and bears the risk of the venture.

questions.q: What is meant by 'adding value'?
options: The difference between the price a business charges and the cost of the inputs it uses
The total amount of money a business receives from sales
The tax a business must pay on its profits
The wages paid to employees for their labour
questions.explain: Added value is the difference between the selling price and the cost of the bought-in inputs used to make a product.

questions.q: A jeweller engraves each customer's name onto their watch free of charge. This is mainly a way of adding value through...
options: creating a unique selling point
reducing variable costs
lowering fixed costs
increasing total revenue only
questions.explain: Personalising the product differentiates it from rivals, giving it a unique selling point that customers value.

questions.q: Which of the following is a reason why new business ideas come about?
options: Products and services becoming obsolete
A permanent fall in all business costs
The removal of all competition from a market
A guarantee of profit from the government
questions.explain: New ideas often arise as existing products become obsolete, technology changes or consumer wants change.

questions.q: What is market segmentation?
options: Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics
The process of selling goods overseas
Reducing the price of a product to attract more customers
Researching a competitor's financial accounts
questions.explain: Segmentation splits a market into groups (e.g. by age, income or lifestyle) so products can be targeted more effectively.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of primary market research?
options: Carrying out a customer questionnaire
Reading a government population report
Using data from a market research company's report
Looking at a competitor's published accounts
questions.explain: Primary research gathers new, first-hand data, for example through questionnaires and surveys.

questions.q: Which of the following would provide qualitative data?
options: Customers' opinions gathered from a focus group
The number of units sold last month
The percentage of customers aged over 40
The total value of sales in a year
questions.explain: Qualitative data describes opinions and attitudes rather than numerical facts.

questions.q: What is a market map (market mapping)?
options: A diagram that plots products against two features to identify gaps in the market
A forecast of a business's future cash flows
A list of all a business's suppliers and customers
A calculation of a business's break-even point
questions.explain: A market map plots products against two variables (e.g. price and quality) to reveal gaps and competitor positions.

questions.q: Which formula correctly calculates total revenue?
options: Selling price × quantity sold
Fixed costs + variable costs
Revenue − total costs
Fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit
questions.explain: Total revenue equals the selling price per unit multiplied by the number of units sold.

questions.q: A business sells 300 units at £8 each. What is its total revenue?
questions.explain: Revenue = price × quantity = £8 × 300 = £2,400.

questions.q: Which formula shows how total costs are calculated?
options: Fixed costs + variable costs
Selling price × quantity
Fixed costs − variable costs
Variable cost per unit ÷ output
questions.explain: Total costs are the sum of fixed costs and total variable costs.

questions.q: A firm has fixed costs of £4,000. Each unit sells for £10 and has a variable cost of £6. How many units must it sell to break even?
options: 1,000 units
400 units
667 units
250 units
questions.explain: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost) = £4,000 ÷ (£10 − £6) = 1,000 units.

questions.q: What is meant by net cash flow?
options: The difference between a business's cash inflows and cash outflows over a period
The total profit a business makes in a year
The amount of money owed to a business by its customers
The value of a business's fixed assets
questions.explain: Net cash flow is the total cash inflows minus the total cash outflows for a given period.

questions.q: What does 'unlimited liability' mean for a sole trader?
options: The owner is personally responsible for all the business's debts
The owner can only lose the amount they invested
The business pays no tax on its profits
The business can sell shares to the public
questions.explain: With unlimited liability there is no legal separation, so the owner's personal assets can be used to pay business debts.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes franchising?
options: Buying the right to trade using an established business's name and business model
Selling shares in a business to the public on the stock market
Two or more people running a business together as partners
A business owned and controlled entirely by the government
questions.explain: A franchisee pays to use the established brand, products and systems of the franchisor.

questions.q: A new bakery decides to sell through a stall in a busy market rather than a high-street shop. This decision mainly concerns which element of the marketing mix?
options: Place
Promotion
Product
Price
questions.explain: 'Place' covers where and how a product is made available to customers.

questions.q: What is a stakeholder?
options: Any individual or group with an interest in, or affected by, a business
A person who owns shares in a public limited company only
A government official who inspects businesses
A customer who has complained about a product
questions.explain: Stakeholders include owners, employees, customers, suppliers, the local community and others affected by the business.

questions.q: Interest rates rise sharply. What is the most likely effect on a small business that relies on a bank loan?
options: Its loan repayments become more expensive
Its loan repayments become cheaper
It pays less tax on its profits
Its exchange rate risk disappears
questions.explain: Higher interest rates increase the cost of borrowing, so repayments on the loan become more expensive.

questions.q: What is inflation?
options: A general and sustained rise in the average price level of goods and services
A fall in the number of people who are unemployed
An increase in a country's exchange rate
A rise in a business's total sales revenue
questions.explain: Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level, which reduces the purchasing power of money.

questions.q: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, goods sold to customers must be...
options: of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described
the cheapest available in the market
produced only within the UK
sold with a lifetime guarantee
questions.explain: Consumer law requires goods to be of satisfactory quality, fit for their purpose and matching their description.
